standard.purpose: The purpose of the standard is to provide individuals with means to proffer their own terms respecting personal privacy, in ways that can be read, acknowledged and agreed to by machines operated by others in the networked world. In a more formal sense, the purpose of the standard is to enable individuals to operate as first parties in agreements with others--mostly companies--operating as second parties.
standard.purposeNote2017: Note that the purpose of this standard is not to address privacy policies, since these are one-sided and need no agreement. (Terms require agreement; privacy policies do not.)
standard.scope: The standard identifies/addresses the manner in which personal privacy terms are proffered and how they can be read and agreed to by machines. The scope of this draft standard is confined to routines in which persons acting as first parties arrive at contractual agreements with organizational entities acting as second-party service providers. It is limited to the selection and signing of a contract kept in a public roster by a neutral noncommercial entity, with identical copies of that contract kept by both parties.

standard.abstract: Contractual interactions and agreements between individuals and the service providers they engage on a network, including websites, applications and AI agents, are covered in this standard. It describes how individuals, acting as first parties, can proffer their privacy requirements as contractual terms and arrive at agreements recorded and kept by both sides. These terms shall be chosen from a collection of standard-form agreements in a roster kept by an independent and neutral non-business entity.(This is similar to how artists might choose Creative Commons licenses allowing or restricting certain kinds of uses for artists' creative work.) Computing devices and software performing as agents for both first and second parties shall engage using any protocol that serves the purpose. The first party shall point to a preferred agreement, or a set of agreements, from which the second party shall accept one. Party-to-party negotiations over terms in any of these contracts or other agreements are outside the scope of this standard. If both parties agree, the chosen contract or agreement shall be signed electronically by both parties or their agents, and a matching record shall be kept by both sides in a form that can be retrieved, audited, or disputed, if necessary, at some later time--and which is available to do so easily.

events.summary: Doc Searls launched ProjectVRM (Vendor Relationship Management) during his Berkman fellowship (2006–2010) to encourage tools that let individuals manage their own relationships with companies. Its stated principles include that customers must be able to proffer their own terms of engagement and keep auditable records of agreements. MyTerms describes ProjectVRM as the place where the ideas behind IEEE 7012 were worked out.
events.significance: Names the two ingredients IEEE 7012 later standardises: person-proffered terms and records kept by both sides.

events.title: Customer Commons spun out to host person-proffered terms
events.place: Customer Commons (spun out of ProjectVRM, Berkman Center), Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Customer Commons was spun out of ProjectVRM as a nonprofit that takes no contributions from commercial entities; it is now a 501(c)(3) (the IRS exemption on record was issued in November 2018). The date is reported inconsistently: in January 2012 ProjectVRM called it 'just in the planning stages', aiming to have it running when The Intention Economy came out that May, and Customer Commons' own website says it was established in 2012, while the MyTerms FAQ dates the spin-off to 2013. MyTerms says it was created to host a roster of standard personal privacy terms, on the model Creative Commons set for copyright licences. Four of its board members — Mary Hodder, Iain Henderson, Joyce Searls and Doc Searls — were involved in IEEE 7012 from the start.

events.title: IEEE approves the P7012 project for machine-readable personal privacy terms
events.place: IEEE Standards Association (IEEE Operations Center), Piscataway, New Jersey
events.summary: The IEEE-SA approved the Project Authorization Request for P7012, Standard for Machine Readable Personal Privacy Terms, on 6 December 2017, after a request dated 16 October 2017. Sponsored by the Social Implications of Technology Standards Committee, with David Reed as working-group chair, it aimed to let individuals act as first parties and companies as second parties, and projected an initial sponsor ballot by July 2019. events.title: Linux Journal pledges to agree to its readers' terms (#NoStalking)
events.place: Cyberlaw Clinic, Harvard Law School, Cambridge, Massachusetts (drafters of the term's legal code)

events.summary: On the ProjectVRM blog Doc Searls summarised the standard: individuals proffer a contract from a list kept by a neutral nonprofit, the company agrees or declines, both sign and keep matching records, and both sides use machine agents. events.title: Searls sketches a 'MyTerms Agreement Record' and compares TCF, Kantara, ISO 27560 and DPV
events.place: Bloomington, Indiana (Ostrom Workshop, Indiana University — author's base)
events.summary: Thinking aloud about a proof of concept, Doc Searls listed three pieces — a browser plug-in, a web-server (CMS) plug-in, and data storage and retrieval. sources.quote: For that combination, we might define a canonical MyTerms Agreement Record, or MAR . Note that this is something I just made up.

issues: All three quotes are verbatim. On 2026-09-23 I fetched the IEEE page fresh, and fetched the projectvrm.org and doc.searls.com posts with curl (the helper gets 403); every --check returned FOUND. The ProjectVRM post is titled 'The MyTerms PAR' and is dated April 6, 2025.

'The form of the shared record is left open' had no source on the record. The MyTerms FAQ says it directly: 'This is an option left open by the MyTerms standard, to maximize development choices'. The claim that the MyTerms Agreement Record is only an idea is supported by Searls: 'Note that this is something I just made up'. His POC post also floats a blockchain log only 'to attract developers who are fond of those'.

The correction slightly overstates the standard's neutrality. The standard does impose requirements: an agreed contract 'shall be signed electronically by both parties or their agents' and 'a matching record shall be kept by both sides'. Neutral on technology is not the same as requiring nothing. I have added this to the correction.

Caveat: the Searls quote on identity ('MyTerms should not be dependent on a universal identity system') is the chair's opinion in a brainstorming post, not the standard's text. The standard's normative text was not read. The protocol-neutral claim rests on the official abstract ('any protocol that serves the purpose') and on the chair's account of the draft.

issues: No error in the correction. On 2026-09-23 I fetched both sources fresh and both --check runs returned FOUND. The FAQ quote keeps the page's typo 'CutomerCommons.org'; it answers 'Can I change my terms for different websites?'.

Two parts of the correction were not covered by the record's quotes: 'on the Creative Commons model' and 'the organisation accepts one of those the person points to'. I have added the standard's own abstract sentences for both.

Nuance for the page. MyData says an organisation can also 'propose an alternative from the same list' or reject, 'and have that recorded as such'. Searls says a person may offer 'a first and second choice of agreement, but no more than that'. Neither contradicts the correction. 'Neutral nonprofit' matches the FAQ; the standard itself says 'independent and neutral non-business entity'.

issues: The verdict (FALSE) and the correction hold. Both quotes are verbatim (re-fetched 2026-09-23, --check FOUND).

The FAQ quote starts with a bare 'No.', so a reader cannot tell what it answers. On the page it answers 'Do I need an AI to use MyTerms?' (FAQ 'For Individuals (The First Party)', item 10). The quote is extended to include the question (--check FOUND).

The correction says AI agents are 'one option the standard leaves open'. That rests on Searls's next sentence, 'The standard leaves these choices open.', which the recorded quote cut off. The quote is extended to include it (--check FOUND). Searls chairs the working group, so an IEEE source is added: the IEEE SA abstract says agents for both parties 'shall engage using any protocol that serves the purpose'. Note that the abstract names AI agents only among the service providers covered (the second-party side). No source says the standard requires AI on the person's side.
The FAQ source's date '2026' is loose. The page's WordPress schema gives datePublished 2025-11-11 and dateModified 2026-01-26, so the date is set to the last-modified date.

issues: Verdict: the claim says 7012 'must be bought'. That is categorically false, because the PDF is free to read and download. 'MISLEADING' understates it, so the verdict is changed to FALSE. The true part (a paid edition also exists) now sits in the correction.

The correction says the free PDF needs 'a free IEEE account'. No source read confirms this. The IEEE GET Program page says only that the program website 'will require users accept of the Terms and Conditions of Use before access to the standard(s) PDF file is permitted'. The Xplore metadata has a getProgramTermsAccepted flag. Neither mentions an account. This is the same finding as the myterms-1 verdict on getProgramNote. The account clause is removed.

The correction says 'printed and store copies are sold', but no source on the record showed that. It is confirmed in the live Accuris store listing, which the 'Purchase' button on the IEEE SA standard page links to (store.accuristech.com/ieee/products/vendor_id/7192). Re-fetched with curl 2026-09-23 (HTTP 200), the raw HTML shows 'Delivery Options PDF Print', 'Price: $80.00', 'Member pricing is available for this product', ISBNs 9798855729450 and 9798855729443, product codes STDGT28515 and STDPD28515. The listing's own description adds '(Note: The PDF of this standard is available at no charge complements of the IEEE GET program ...)'. The helper returns NOT-FOUND for these strings because they are outside its extracted tags, so the listing cannot be added as a checked source. The finding is recorded here, and the correction's wording stays general (no price).

The quote on source 1 ('"publicationDate":"20 January 2026"') does not support the claim that the PDF is free. The same page's abstract metadata carries IEEE's own no-charge note, so that is now the quote.
